_meta.description: Canonical claims ledger, aggregated from docs/claims/guides/*.json by scripts/claims-extract.mjs. Edit the shards, not this file.

claims.text: Apply a bulk adjustment
Replace or shift the targets of many stations at once.
Change the Target VWC of many stations at once, either by replacing every value or by shifting them all by the same amount.
Table toolbar › Bulk Adjust
Bulk Adjust edits Target VWC, not the percent adjustment.
The button stays disabled until at least one row checkbox is ticked.
Select the stations
Tick the checkbox on each station row.
Ticking an area or hole row cascades the selection to everything beneath it, so you can take a whole hole in one click.
Five stations selected.
The Bulk Adjust link above the table becomes active.
Open Bulk Adjust
The link sits above the table beside the threshold filter.
The dialog opens with the count of stations you selected at the top — check it before going further.
Bulk Adjust dialog.
The count confirms your selection.
Choose replace or shift
Replace overwrites every selected station with the value you enter.
Shift moves each station up or down by that amount, keeping the differences between them.
Shift is the safer choice when the stations were individually tuned.
Shift by −5 percent, preserving the relative targets.
Apply to all
Apply to all writes the new targets and closes the dialog.
The suggested percentages recalculate against the new targets straight away, so the Suggested column will move.
Targets updated; suggestions recalculated against them.
On failure. A bulk adjust error means some values may already have been written.
Check the column before retrying rather than applying twice.
Target VWC changed on every station you selected and on none that you did not.
The Suggested column moved to reflect the new targets.
The Push Changes count in the toolbar reflects the new pending edits.
Calculation methods
How the two available algorithms differ.
Two algorithms can produce the suggested percentage.
They use different inputs and behave differently.
Settings › Calculation
The dropdown labels the two methods Option 1 and Option 2, and describes neither.
The selector is hidden in production unless the site is already set to Option 1.
The default is Option 2, the delta-plus-today’s-ET method.
Find the selector
Suggested Percent Adjust Calculation is the first field on the Calculation tab.
On a production site it only appears when the persisted algorithm is already Option 1, so most users never see it.
The dropdown offers only Option 1 and Option 2; nothing in the product says what either one does.
The algorithm dropdown, above the three amounts.
Option 2 — delta plus today’s ET, the default

The server computes it per station: target minus working VWC gives a deficit, the deficit becomes an amount of water, today’s ET adjusted by the crop coefficient is added, the daily maximum caps the total, and the result is divided by the Lynx reference amount.
Every suggestion in this column came from that chain.
Option 1 — ratio of target to measured
Option 1 multiplies the percent adjust Lynx currently holds by target divided by measured moisture, and rounds.
It uses no ET, no reference amount and no cap, so Max Amount and Lynx Reference Amount are disabled while it is selected.
With Option 1 selected, the two amount fields are disabled.
Consequence. Because Option 1 scales the current Lynx value, a station sitting at 0 percent adjust stays at 0 no matter how dry it is.
The cap is what makes them look different
Option 2 flattens everything above the daily maximum onto one number.
Option 1 has no ceiling, so its suggestions spread out — and can go far higher than you intend on a station that reads very dry.
Runs of identical values are a signature of the capped method.
Switching is a course-wide change
Saving a different algorithm recalculates every station and reloads the dashboard.
Review the whole Suggested column before pushing anything after a switch.
Compare the column before and after switching, not one row.
You can say which algorithm your site uses.
You know why Max Amount is greyed out under Option 1.
Calculation questions
Identical suggestions, missing values, stale scans.
Identical suggestions, missing values and stale scans — three things that look like bugs and are not.
Table and Settings
All three have the same first check: is the number a measurement, a model, or nothing at all?
Identical suggestions across many stations
When the required amount exceeds the daily maximum, every station above the cap lands on the same percentage.
A run of identical numbers means the cap is deciding, not the scan.
A run of identical values is the cap, not a fault.
Work out your own ceiling
The maximum possible suggestion is the daily maximum divided by the Lynx reference amount.
Change either number and the ceiling moves — which is the honest fix if the ceiling is too low for your course.
Max Amount over Lynx Reference Amount sets the ceiling.
Example. A 10 mm cap against a 3 mm reference gives 333 percent.
Raising the cap to 12 mm gives 400.
A dash instead of a number
A dash means there is nothing to show: no current scan and no modelled value either.
It is not zero, and it is not an error in the calculation — the station has no data to calculate from.
Where a value is absent the column shows a dash, not a zero.
Grey italics mean modelled
A greyed, italic average means the value came from the model rather than a scan taken that day.
The calculation still runs, but it is running on an estimate.
A modelled value: grey and italic.
If the whole course is stale, check the source
The diagnostics dialog reports whether the organisation has TurfRad access, whether it has scan data at all, and the last scan date.
A course-wide problem is almost always here rather than in your settings.
If TurfRad access and scan data are both fine and only the date is old, request a fresh scan from the toolbar rather than waiting for one.
Diagnostics: TurfRad access, scan data, last scan date.
You can explain a run of identical suggestions.
You can tell a dash from a zero.
You know today’s last scan date.
Calculation settings
Max Amount, Lynx Reference Amount and Crop Coefficient.
Three numbers decide every suggestion on the course: the daily maximum, the Lynx reference amount, and the crop coefficient.
Settings › Calculation
These are site-level settings — they apply to every user on the site.
Changing any of them recalculates every suggestion and reloads the dashboard.
Open Settings on the Calculation tab
The gear button opens the dialog on Calculation by default.
If you last arrived through Review Threshold it opens on Minimum Threshold instead — the tab is sticky for the rest of the session.
Settings dialog, Calculation tab.
Daily Max Amount caps the water
The most water Spatial Adjust will ask for in one day, in your own units, up to a hard ceiling of 15.
Every station whose deficit exceeds this lands on the same suggested percentage, which is why identical numbers appear in runs.
Daily Max Amount, edited in the units your preferences specify.
Stored in millimetres. The backend keeps these amounts in millimetres and the dialog converts on the way in and out — two decimals imperial, one metric.
Lynx Reference Amount is what 100% means
This is the amount of water a station applies at 100 percent adjust.
The suggested percentage is the applied amount divided by this reference.
Set it too low and every suggestion looks enormous.
Lynx Reference Amount, ceiling of 10.
Worked example. A 10 mm cap against a 3 mm reference gives a maximum suggestion of 333 percent — the ceiling you see repeated across a dry course.
Crop Coefficient scales today’s ET
A whole-number percentage from 0 to 200 applied to the day’s ET before it enters the calculation.
Below 100 the course is treated as using less water than reference ET suggests; above 100, more.
Crop Coefficient: 0 to 200, integers.
Saving recalculates the whole course
Save Changes sends the settings, asks the server to recalculate adjustments, and reloads the dashboard so that area and hole averages are rebuilt.
Expect the Suggested column to move on every row.
After a recalculation the dashboard reloads with new suggestions.
You can state what 100 percent adjust means on your site in inches or millimetres.
You know which setting produces a run of identical suggestions.
Creating profiles
Capture the current targets under a name.
Capture the station targets you have tuned, under a name you will recognise next season.
Settings › Target Profiles
Target Profiles is still in development and is not in the shipping build yet.
The screens here show a proposed design; the tab being built lists five named profile slots, so what you see on your own screen may differ.
A profile stores one Target VWC per station and nothing else — no percent adjustments, no enable states.
Tune the targets first
A profile is a snapshot, so the work happens in the table before you save anything.
Get the course reading the way you want it, hole by hole, and only then capture it.
The Target VWC column is what a profile would capture.
Open the Target Profiles tab
Profiles sit with the calculation settings rather than in the table, because a target set is a calculation input rather than a station edit.
Proposed Target Profiles tab.
Name it for the condition
Name a profile for the reason the targets are what they are — Summer Baseline, Tournament Week, Overseed Recovery.
A date tells you when; a condition tells you why, which is what you will be searching for.
Three profiles, one active.
Check the station count
The count beside each profile says how many stations it covers.
A profile captured while the course was partly disabled covers fewer stations than the course has, and applying it later leaves the rest untouched.
Coverage is part of what a profile is.
The new profile appears in the list with today’s date and the full station count.
The targets in the table are unchanged by saving.
Dashboard overview
The four regions of the screen and what each one is telling you.
The whole feature lives on one screen.
Learn what each of the four regions tells you, and which numbers are measured versus calculated.
/spatialadjust
You need a Spatial Adjust account on a site with TurfRad scan data.
Without recent scans the map and table are empty.
The route is all lowercase — /spatialadjust. /spatialAdjust does not resolve and redirects to the error page.
The view is desktop and tablet only; phones are turned away by the route guard.
Start with the toolbar
The left of the toolbar identifies where you are: site name, and a course selector that only appears when the site has more than one Lynx course.
Next to it the weather strip shows current temperature, relative humidity, today’s ET and precipitation.
It reports conditions; it is not where the suggested percentages come from.
Option 1 uses no ET at all, and Option 2’s figure is calculated before the page loads.
Toolbar, left: site, course selector, weather strip and the course-wide moisture summary.
Note. Avg / High / Low moisture are computed across every station in the selected course, not just the ones visible in the table.
Read the map
Every station is a pin coloured by its latest measured VWC against the four moisture bands in the legend.
Drag the handles on the colour bar to move the band boundaries — the map recolours immediately and the change is saved to your user preferences.
Map with the moisture legend.
Bands default to 0–5, 6–19, 20–30 and above 30 percent.
Variance view. The button beside the legend switches the pins from absolute moisture to variance — how far each station sits from its target rather than its raw reading.
Use the chart for one area at a time
The chart above the table plots the holes you pick in the multiselect.
Selecting a row in the table changes the chart header to that area or hole and its average moisture, so the chart and the table always describe the same thing.
Chart and table share a selection.
The header reads the selected item and its average moisture.
Work in the table
The table is a drill-down: course, then areas, then holes, then stations.
Breadcrumbs at the top left take you back up.
At station level you get the editable columns — Target VWC, the current and suggested adjustment side by side, your own % Adj. value, and the Enable switch.
Station-level rows for hole 3 of area AP.
Measured or modelled. A greyed, italic Avg.
VWC with a calculator icon means the value was estimated from the model rather than measured by a scan that day.
Check the counts before you leave
The right of the toolbar is your work queue.
Push Changes counts stations with an unpushed edit, and the green counter beside it counts stations already pushed today.
When both are quiet, there is nothing outstanding.
Six stations pending, six already pushed today.
With nothing pending the button is disabled.
The map, chart and table all name the same course.
Calculation ET under the filter tabs is the figure the calculation used.
The weather strip reports current conditions separately, so do not expect the two to agree.
The station count on the All Stations tab matches the number of pins on the map.
Editing station targets
Change one station’s Target VWC and see the effect.
Change one station’s target and watch what it does to the suggestion.
Table, Target VWC column
Target VWC accepts whole numbers from 0 to 50.
A target change recalculates that station’s suggestion; it does not push anything.
Drill down to the station
The table drills from course to areas, then holes, then stations.
Breadcrumbs at the top left take you back up a level.
The flat All Stations tab is faster when you already know the station name.
Hole rows for area AP.
Clicking one shows its stations.
Type the new target
The Target VWC field takes a whole number between 0 and 50.
Raising it increases the deficit and therefore the suggestion; lowering it does the opposite.
Target VWC on station 9AP1.
Read the new suggestion
The Suggested column recalculates against the new target.
If it lands on the same number as its neighbours, the daily maximum is capping it rather than the target deciding it.
Suggested follows the target you just set.
Override the percentage if you need to
The % Adj. field is separate from the target and accepts 0 to 900.
Editing it queues the station for push and leaves the suggestion visible underneath for comparison.
The pending icon marks a station queued for push.
Which to change. Edit the target when the station should always be wetter or drier.
Edit % Adj. when today is unusual.
The target shows the value you typed.
The suggestion recalculated.
The station appears in the Push Changes count only if you edited % Adj.
Enable and disable stations
Cascading enable state across areas, holes and stations.
Take a station, hole or area out of adjustment — and understand what cascading does before you confirm it.
Table, Enable column
A disabled station is excluded from adjustment entirely; it is not sent a zero, it is simply not sent.
Toggle a single station
The switch in the Enable column takes effect on that station alone.
Station 5AP1 is off here, which is why it has no pending adjustment however dry it reads.
A disabled station: the switch on its row is grey.
Toggling a parent cascades
Hole and area rows carry the same switch, and turning one off turns off everything beneath it.
That is usually what you want when a hole is out of play.
Hole rows carry their own Enable switch.
Confirm the cascade
Because a cascade can affect dozens of heads, Spatial Adjust asks first and names the scope: this hole and every station beneath it.
Continue applies it; Cancel leaves everything as it was.
The cascade confirmation names exactly what will change.
Silence the prompt once you trust it
The checkbox suppresses the confirmation for future cascades.
It is stored in your own preferences, so it hides the prompt for you and not for your colleagues.
The same dialog for an area-level enable.
Careful. With the prompt suppressed, an area-level toggle silently changes every hole and station under it.
Check the result on the map
Switch Layers to Enabled Stations to see only the heads still in adjustment.
Anything that disappeared is out — deliberately or otherwise.
Layers filtered to enabled stations only.
The stations you meant to disable show a grey switch.
The Push Changes count dropped by the pending edits you just excluded.
Filter by % Adj.
Find the outliers at both ends before you push.
The Over/Under filter finds the extremes at both ends at once.
It is not a range, and reading it as one will mislead you.
Table toolbar
The filter reads the suggested percentage, and only for stations that are enabled.
A disabled station never appears in it however extreme its number.
Read the two tabs
All Stations carries the full count.
Beside it, the Over/Under tab carries the count of stations the filter currently catches.
Until you set a filter that count is a dash and the tab does nothing — it is not broken, there is simply nothing to show yet.
Two tabs: All Stations, and the Over/Under count.
Open the options
The link to the right of the table toolbar states the thresholds currently in force — % ADJ.
OVER 200%, UNDER 10% — so you can read the filter without opening it.
Clicking it opens Over/Under Options.
The link doubles as a readout of the current thresholds.
Set the two ends independently
Over accepts 0 to 300 and defaults to 200.
Under accepts 0 to 100 and defaults to 10.
Each has its own checkbox, so you can run one end without the other — Over alone to find the stations asking for far too much, Under alone to find the ones asking for almost nothing.
Over/Under Options.
Each threshold has its own checkbox.
It catches both extremes, not a band
A station is caught if its suggestion is above the Over value OR below the Under value.
With 200 and 10 set you get everything over 200 percent and everything under 10 percent — and nothing in between.
It is an outlier finder.
Reading it as “between 10 and 200” gives you exactly the stations it is not showing you.
The filtered tab: the extremes at both ends, not the middle.
Why it matters. These are the two lists worth a second look before a push: the ones about to get a great deal of water, and the ones about to get almost none.
Exclude Zeros belongs to Under
Exclude Zeros is greyed out until Under is enabled, because a zero is below any under-threshold and the option means nothing without one.
Tick it and genuine zeros drop out of the filter, leaving the stations that asked for a little rather than the ones that asked for nothing.
Your thresholds are saved to your own user preferences, not to the site.
Exclude Zeros is disabled until Under is on.
Not the same setting. Settings › Minimum Threshold has its own Exclude Zeros.
That one changes what gets written to Lynx at push time.
This one only changes which rows you are looking at.
You can state that the filter is an OR across both ends, not a range.
You know the Over/Under count reads as a dash until a filter is set.
You know which Exclude Zeros changes the push and which only changes the view.
Map navigation
Pan, zoom, layers, and switching between moisture and variance.
Read the pins, move the moisture bands, switch to variance, and filter what the map shows.
Map panel
Band boundaries and the variance view are saved to your own user preferences, not to the site.
Pins are coloured by measured moisture
Every station is a pin placed at its real coordinates and filled with the colour of the moisture band its latest reading falls into.
Four bands by default: 0–5, 6–19, 20–30, and above 30 percent.
The course, coloured by measured moisture.
Move the band boundaries
The colour bar under the legend has draggable handles.
Move one and the map recolours as you drag — useful when your course sits mostly inside one band and everything looks the same colour.
Dragging a handle changes the boundary and saves it to your preferences.
Switch to variance
The button beside the legend toggles between VWC and variance.
Variance colours each pin by how far it sits from its own target instead of by its raw reading, which is the view you want when targets differ across the course.
Variance view: three bands, centred on target.
Filter with Layers
Layers chooses which stations are drawn: all of them, or only the enabled ones.
Disabled stations are not being adjusted, so hiding them leaves only the heads your push will affect.
Layers, with All Stations and Enabled Stations.
Map and table stay in sync
Selecting a station in the table highlights it on the map, and selecting a pin selects the row.
Use whichever is faster to find the head you mean.
One selection, shown in both panels.
You can recolour the map by moving a band handle.
You can switch between moisture and variance.
Layers hides disabled stations.
Set a minimum threshold
Keep trivial adjustments from reaching Lynx.
Stop trivial adjustments reaching Lynx.
Set the percentage below which a suggestion is either zeroed or lifted to the threshold value.
Settings › Minimum Threshold
The threshold is a site-level setting.
It applies to every user on the site, not just you.
It is applied at push time, not at calculation time — the table keeps showing the raw suggested value.
Setting the percentage to 0 disables the feature entirely.
Open Settings
The gear button at the right of the toolbar opens the settings dialog.
It opens on whichever tab you last arrived at, so it may not open on Calculation.
The gear button in the toolbar’s right-hand button group.
Choose the Minimum Threshold tab
The left rail lists the settings groups.
Minimum Threshold sits second, under Calculation.
Settings dialog, Minimum Threshold tab.
Enter the percentage
Type the cutoff as a whole number between 0 and 50.
Ten percent is a common starting point: it removes the noise from stations that are already close to target while leaving genuine corrections intact.
Threshold set to 10 percent.
No server-side check. The 0–50 bound is enforced by the dialog only.
Values sent by other means are not validated on the server.
Decide what happens below the line
Set to zero skips the station entirely — Lynx receives 0%.
Set to the minimum threshold value raises the suggestion up to the threshold instead, so the station still gets a small run.
Exclude Zeros, available only on the second option, leaves genuine zeros at zero rather than lifting them.
Below-threshold behaviour, with the second option selected.
Save and confirm at push time
Saving a threshold-only change does not reload the dashboard — the pending push list is simply recalculated.
Open Push Changes and the pink banner tells you how many stations the threshold touched, with each affected row showing its original value and the adjusted one.
Push dialog.
Two stations were lifted to the threshold; the original and adjusted values are shown together.
The push dialog names the number of stations the threshold adjusted.
Rows below the threshold show an arrow and the adjusted percentage in pink.
Reopening Settings shows the value you saved, not the previous one.
Preferences
Language, units, temperature scale and number formatting.
Language, units, temperature and number formatting.
These belong to you, not to the site.
Settings › Preferences
Preferences are stored against your user account; the calculation settings on the other tabs are stored against the site.
Open the Preferences tab
Preferences is the last entry in the settings rail.
Nothing here changes a single suggested percentage — it changes how numbers are presented to you.
Settings dialog, Preferences tab.
Units of Measure changes what you type
The stored amounts are millimetres.
Switching to imperial shows them in inches, with two decimal places and a hundredth-of-an-inch step; metric gets one decimal place and a tenth-of-a-millimetre step.
That conversion runs when the dialog opens, not when you change the setting.
Units of Measure drives the labels and precision on the Calculation tab.

Check after switching. Changing Units of Measure and saving in the same visit does not re-convert the amounts already on the Calculation tab — they are saved as though they were already in the new unit, which rescales them by 25.4.
After a unit change, save, then reopen Settings and check Max Amount and Lynx Reference Amount before you push anything.
Language applies immediately
Saving a new language re-applies translations across the site without a reload, and refetches your user record so the choice sticks on your next visit.
Language, units, temperature scale and separator.
Temperature and separator affect the toolbar
Temperature scale changes the weather strip; the group and decimal separator changes how every number on the screen is punctuated, which matters most in the dense table columns.
The weather strip follows your temperature scale.
Amount fields on the Calculation tab show the unit you chose.
The weather strip shows your temperature scale.
Push failures
Reading the failure count and retrying safely.
Read the failure count, understand what has already been tried, and re-push only what failed.
Push progress dialog
By the time you see a failure, Spatial Adjust has already retried the affected stations twice.
Read the count, not the colour
The message names how many stations could not be updated.
The rest of the push succeeded — a failure is partial, and the stations that verified are already live in Lynx.
Two stations could not be updated.
The other four are done.
Know what has already been tried
Failed stations are re-pushed automatically, up to two further attempts.
Pushing again by hand immediately afterwards is a fourth attempt at the same connection, which rarely behaves differently.
The automatic retry pass, before the failure is reported.
The bar restarts at zero and counts only the stations being retried.
Check the connection to Lynx
Diagnostics reports the Lynx interconnect, whether the cloud can be pinged, and the installation and course identifiers.
If the ping is failing, no amount of re-pushing will help.
Diagnostics: Lynx interconnect, ping, installation ID.
Also worth checking. When the connection drops, a banner appears above the toolbar and percent adjust values can be neither read nor written.
Re-push only the failures
The stations that failed are still pending, so reopening Push Changes offers exactly them.
Untick anything that already went out rather than sending the whole set a second time.
The failed stations are still queued; the successful ones are not.
You know how many stations failed and which they were.
Diagnostics confirms Lynx is reachable before you retry.
The retry contained only the failed stations.
Push changes to Lynx
Review, deselect, send and verify.
Review every pending adjustment, drop the ones you do not want, and send the rest to the controller.
Toolbar › Push Changes
Lynx must be reachable.
If the connection is lost an amber banner appears above the toolbar and percent adjust values cannot be read or written.
Stations already pushed today are listed separately and arrive unselected, so you do not adjust the same head twice.
Check the pending count
The button reads the number of stations with an unpushed edit.
Beside it the green counter shows how many have already gone out today.
If Push Changes is greyed out there is nothing queued.
Six changes pending, six already pushed today.
Review the two lists
The dialog puts the current value on the left and the change on the right.
Available to Push comes first, with everything ticked; Pushed Today follows, unticked.
Tick a pushed station only if you genuinely mean to adjust it a second time today.
Push dialog.
Current on the left, the proposed change on the right.
Look for threshold adjustments
If a minimum threshold is set, a pink banner counts the stations it altered and each affected row shows the original percentage and the value that will actually be sent.
Review Threshold opens Settings on the threshold tab if the numbers look wrong.
Two stations were adjusted by the minimum threshold before sending.
Untick anything you are not sure about
The footer button counts only the ticked rows.
Unticking is not the same as reverting — the station keeps its edited value in the table and will be offered again next time.
The footer button always names the number of changes that will be sent.
Send and watch the progress
Spatial Adjust first re-reads the current adjustments from Lynx for comparison, then writes station by station, then verifies.
Failed stations are retried automatically before the run is declared finished.
Push in progress, station four of six.
Confirm the result
A successful run confirms every selected change reached Lynx.
A failure names the number of stations that could not be updated — check the Lynx connection and push those again rather than the whole set.
All selected changes pushed successfully.
The Push Changes button is disabled and the pending count is zero.
The green pushed-today counter increased by the number you sent.
Pushed rows in the table now show the pushed icon rather than the pending one.
Get fresh scan data
Request a new TurfRad scan rather than waiting for one.
A stale course is not something you have to wait out.
Request a new TurfRad scan, and reload when it lands.
Toolbar
When a scan is not current the calculation still runs — it runs on a modelled value carried forward from the last scan and the weather since, shown in grey italics.
Read the scan date before anything else
Every station row carries the date its reading was captured.
One stale row is a station; a column of stale dates is the whole course, and that is a supply problem rather than a settings problem.
Scan dates sit beside the station name in the table.
Request the latest scan
The circular-arrow button in the toolbar’s right-hand group is Request latest scan data.
It asks TurfRad for a new scan; it does not reload the dashboard, and it does not change a single calculation setting.
Request latest scan data, between the pushed-today counter and the gear.
Note. This button and Reload Data are two different things.
One asks for new data; the other brings data that has already arrived into the page.
It queues, it does not block
The request is queued and you are told so: retrieval may take several minutes, and you are notified when it is ready.
You can carry on reading the table while it runs — nothing is frozen and nothing is lost if you navigate away.
A queued request confirms immediately; the data arrives later.
Reload when the banner appears
When the scan lands, a banner says so.
Reload Data pulls it into the dashboard and every suggestion recalculates against the new readings.
Dismiss closes the banner and leaves you on the data you already had — the new scan is not thrown away, it is simply not loaded yet.
The banner offers Reload Data or Dismiss.
Careful. Dismissing is not declining.
The next reload picks the new scan up.
If the request will not queue
A failed request says so straight away rather than silently doing nothing.

If it keeps failing, the diagnostics dialog reports whether the organisation has TurfRad access and whether it has scan data at all — a course-wide problem is almost always there rather than in your settings.
Diagnostics: TurfRad access, scan data, last scan date.
You know the toolbar can request a scan, not only display the last one.
You can tell Request latest scan data from Reload Data.
You know Dismiss leaves the dashboard on the data it already had.
Reviewing changes
Reading the two lists in the push dialog.
Read the push dialog properly before you send: two lists, two columns, and one count that matters.
Push Changes dialog
Everything in the dialog is still reversible.
Nothing is written until you use the footer button.
Open Push Changes
The button carries the number of stations with an unpushed edit.
It is disabled when nothing is queued, so a greyed-out button means there is nothing to review.
Six changes pending.
Read Current against Changes
The left column is what Lynx holds now; the right is what will replace it.
Both name the station, so you are always comparing the same head across the row.
Current on the left, the proposed change on the right.
Treat the two lists differently
Available to Push comes first, ticked.
Pushed Today follows, unticked, and is there to stop you adjusting the same head twice in a day.
That hold releases at midnight where the course is, not 24 hours after the push.
Tick a pushed station only when you mean to.
Pushed Today arrives unselected by design.
Check for threshold rewrites
When a minimum threshold is set, the banner counts the stations it will rewrite and the affected rows show both the original and the value that will actually be sent.
Two stations will be rewritten by the threshold rules.
Trust the footer count
The footer button names the number of ticked rows, and that is exactly what will be sent.
Unticking a row is not the same as reverting it — the edit stays in the table for next time.
The footer count is the contract.
The footer count matches the rows you ticked.
No station in Pushed Today is ticked unless you meant it.
Managing seasonal profiles
A profile per season and per event.
A small set of profiles, one per condition, is easier to run a season with than a long list of dated snapshots.
Settings › Target Profiles
Target Profiles is still in development and is not in the shipping build yet.
The screens here show a proposed design; the tab being built lists five named profile slots, so what you see on your own screen may differ.
Applying a profile is a course-wide recalculation, so treat it as a planned change rather than a quick switch.
Keep the list short
Three or four profiles covers most courses: a summer baseline, a shoulder-season set, a tournament set, and a recovery set for after aeration or overseed.
A short list stays readable a year later.
Apply the evening before
Applying rewrites every target and recalculates every suggestion.

Find the two adjustment columns
Current is the percent adjust Lynx holds for the station right now.
Suggested is what Spatial Adjust calculated from this morning’s scan.
The gap between them is the change you are being asked to make.
Current and Suggested sit side by side under the Adjustment heading.
Read it against Avg. VWC and Target VWC

The calculation starts from the difference between measured moisture and the station target, converts that into an amount of water, adds today’s ET, and expresses the result as a percentage of the Lynx reference amount.
A station well under target asks for more water; one over target asks for less.
Station 3AP1 measured 27.6 percent against a 54 percent target — the largest deficit on the hole.
Notice where suggestions cluster
Several stations show the same suggested value.
That is the daily Max Amount cap: once the required amount exceeds the cap, every station above it lands on the same percentage.
If most of your course reads identically, the cap is doing the deciding, not the scan.
A run of identical suggestions is the signature of the Max Amount cap.
What to do. Raise Daily Max Amount in Settings › Calculation, or accept that the course is being deliberately limited.

Settings › Minimum Threshold
The threshold is applied when you push, not when the suggestion is calculated.

Choose what below-threshold means
Set to zero skips the station: Lynx receives 0 percent.
Set to the minimum threshold value lifts the suggestion up to the threshold so the station still gets a short run.

Available only under the second option: a station whose suggestion is a true zero stays at zero instead of being lifted to the threshold.

Understand Spatial Adjust
Where moisture scans come from and what the feature does with them.
What the feature actually does: turn yesterday’s moisture scan into today’s percent adjustment, and write it to Lynx.
/spatialadjust
Spatial Adjust is a feature of IntelliDash, not a separate product.
Reaching it means logging into IntelliDash.
Access is granted per user, and the view is admitted only on desktop and tablet.
It lives inside IntelliDash
The route is /spatialadjust, all lowercase, inside the IntelliDash site.
A camelCase URL does not resolve — it redirects to the generic error page.
Access is checked per user before the view loads.
The Spatial Adjust header, inside IntelliDash.
TurfRad supplies the measurement
Each station’s Avg.
VWC comes from a TurfRad moisture scan — the mean volumetric water content measured across the station, with the date it was captured beside the station name.
Measured moisture and its scan date, per station.
You supply the target
Target VWC is the moisture you want that station to hold.
It is yours to set, station by station, between 0 and 50 percent.
The gap between measured and target is what the calculation works on.
Target VWC is an editable input, not a reading.
Spatial Adjust does the arithmetic

The difference between target and measured moisture becomes an amount of water, today’s ET is added, the daily maximum caps it, and the result is divided by the Lynx reference amount to give a percentage.
The Suggested column is the output of that chain.
In one line. Suggested % = the applied amount ÷ the Lynx reference amount × 100, rounded.
Lynx runs the water
Spatial Adjust never waters anything.
It writes a percent adjust value onto each station in Lynx, and Lynx applies that percentage to the station’s programmed run time.
Nothing changes until you push.
Push Changes is the only thing that writes to the controller.
You can name the three inputs: measured VWC, target VWC and today’s ET.
You know that nothing reaches Lynx until Push Changes is used.
Understanding VWC
Measured, modelled and target volumetric water content.
Three different numbers wear the label VWC.
Knowing which one you are reading explains most surprises.
Table, Avg. VWC and Target VWC
VWC is volumetric water content, expressed as a percentage of soil volume.
Measured: the scan mean
When the scan date is today, Avg.
VWC is the mean moisture TurfRad measured across that station.
It is a measurement, and it is the number the calculation prefers.
A current scan: black text, today’s date.
Modelled: the fallback
When the scan is not current, Spatial Adjust falls back to a modelled value carried forward from the last scan and the weather since.
It is shown in grey italics so you can tell it apart at a glance.
Station 7AP1 has no current scan; the value shown is modelled.
Target: your input
Target VWC is a whole number from 0 to 50 that you set per station.
Higher targets ask for more water.
It is the only VWC on the row you can type into.
Target VWC accepts 0 to 50, integers only.
The delta is what drives the suggestion
Subtract the working VWC from the target and you have the deficit the calculation must close.
Add today’s ET, cap it at the daily maximum, and express it against the Lynx reference amount.
Target minus measured, per station, is the whole idea.
Aggregate rows average their children
At hole and area level the same two columns show averages rather than readings, and the scan date column shows the most recent scan beneath that row.
An italic average means at least one child is modelled.
Hole rows: average measured, average target, latest scan.
You can tell a measured value from a modelled one without checking the date.

Verify results
Confirming Lynx accepted every adjustment.
A push is four phases, not one.
Knowing them tells you whether a slow run is working or stuck.
Push progress dialog
Verification is automatic.
You do not have to check Lynx by hand to know whether a push landed.
It writes first, station by station
Nothing is read before the push begins.
Stations are written in sequence with a short pause between each, and the progress line names which one it is on.
On a large course this is the slowest phase, and a stalled counter here means the connection, not the calculation.
Phase one: writing, four of six.
Then it reads Lynx back
With the writing done, Spatial Adjust retrieves the current percent adjustments from Lynx.
This is a read-back, not a baseline — it is collecting what Lynx actually holds now so the next phase has something to check the push against.
Phase two: reading back what Lynx now holds.
Then it verifies
Spatial Adjust re-reads the station list and compares each value it sent against what Lynx now reports.
Anything that does not match is treated as failed rather than assumed good.
Phase three: comparing what Lynx reports against what was sent.
Failures are retried automatically
Stations that did not take are re-pushed, up to two further attempts after the first.
The progress line names how many are being retried, so a retry is information rather than an error.
The bar restarts at zero for the retry pass and counts only the failed stations, so a drop from nearly complete back to nothing is the retry beginning, not the push collapsing.
Phase four: retrying the stations that did not verify.
Read the outcome
A clean run confirms that every selected change reached Lynx and verified.
Back on the dashboard the pending count is zero and the pushed-today counter has grown by what you sent.
All selected changes pushed and verified.
The dialog reported success rather than a failure count.
The pending count is zero and the pushed-today counter increased.
